01.title: What if learning felt like Duolingo, but for anything?
01.author: Dierta Pasific
01.markdown:
### I built Beacon — an AI-powered learning app that generates a personalized curriculum for any skill you want to learn.

There’s a specific kind of guilt that comes with an unfinished Udemy course.

You bought it during a sale, told yourself this time would be different, got maybe two hours in, and then life happened. The tab is still pinned. You haven’t opened it in three months. Sound familiar?

Or maybe you tried the other direction — no course, just vibes. You googled “how to learn machine learning” and got fourteen contradictory Reddit threads, a Medium post from 2019, and a GitHub repo with no README. You closed the tab after twenty minutes feeling more lost than when you started.

Most learning content sits at one of two extremes: the firehose or the void. Either it’s a 40-hour course that assumes you have unlimited time and infinite motivation, or it’s scattered resources that assume you already know where to start. Neither works for most people.

That’s the problem [Beacon](https://beaconlearn.vercel.app/) is trying to solve.

## Duolingo’s Secret Isn’t the Content

Duolingo doesn’t succeed because its Spanish lessons are the best Spanish lessons ever written. They’re fine. What Duolingo cracked is the *habit loop* — tiny daily sessions, a streak you emotionally don’t want to break, visible progress, a satisfying little dopamine hit every time you complete a lesson.

The format is what keeps people coming back. Not the content.

So the question Beacon started with was: what if you took that format and made it work for *any* skill? Not just languages. Rust ownership. Negotiation tactics. Watercolor painting. Grant writing. Personal finance. Whatever you actually want to learn.

The reason nobody had done this before is that building curricula is expensive. Duolingo has teams of linguists and educators designing every lesson. You can’t do that for every possible subject. But LLMs change that equation entirely — generating a structured, personalized curriculum is now a one-API-call problem.

So the interesting question stopped being “can we generate lessons?” and became: **can we wrap those lessons in a loop that makes someone come back tomorrow?**

## How Beacon Works

Onboarding takes about 60 seconds.

You type in a skill — anything, seriously, try something niche — your current level, how many hours a week you can realistically commit, and optionally a goal you’re working toward. A career switcher learning Python to build a portfolio gets a different path than a curious person who just wants to understand how it works. Beacon accounts for that from the start.

From there, Gemini generates your learning path — but not all at once. Phase 1 is ready in about 15 to 20 seconds. As you work through it, the next phase is quietly generated in the background, so by the time you finish your current lessons, the next ones are already waiting. It feels instant. The structure is six lesson formats depending on what you’re learning — a concept card for new ideas, an analogy for abstract concepts, a code snippet for technical topics, a myth-vs-reality card for correcting misconceptions, a did-you-know for engagement, and a flashcard for review. Every single one ends with a quiz.

Each phase is generated once and cached. So the AI cost is paid upfront, and serving lessons after that is essentially free.

## The Loop That Makes It Stick

Here’s where it gets Duolingo-brained, intentionally.

Every lesson you complete earns XP. XP drives you through 50 levels. Completing your lesson for the day keeps your streak alive — miss a day and it resets to zero. Do more than your daily minimum and you earn bonus XP at 1.5x. Hit a milestone — a 7-day streak, level 10, five perfect quizzes in a row — and you unlock an achievement.

None of this is subtle. It’s a deliberate borrowing of mechanics that are proven to work. But here’s the thing: they work because they tap into something real. A streak isn’t really about the app. It’s about identity. You’re not protecting your Beacon streak. You’re protecting the version of yourself that learns every day. That’s a harder thing to quit.

The quiz design reinforces this. Every micro-lesson ends with two or three questions — instant feedback, explanation shown whether you got it right or wrong, a hint system if you’re stuck. After every five lessons there’s a checkpoint quiz. Weekly recaps cover everything from the past seven days. Spaced repetition schedules reviews at 1, 3, 7, 14, and 30 days after you first complete a lesson. The goal isn’t just to expose you to information. It’s to make it stick.

## Any Skill, Actually

The “any skill” part is worth taking seriously, because it’s easy to dismiss as marketing.

Most learning platforms have 30 to 50 topics, heavily weighted toward tech and business. If you want to learn Python, you’re well served. If you want to learn how to write grants for nonprofits, or understand Byzantine history, or get better at conflict resolution, you’re on your own.

Beacon doesn’t have a topic list. There is no catalogue. You type what you want to learn and it builds the path. That’s a genuinely different kind of product — one where the coverage is unlimited by design, not by the number of educators you’ve hired.

The people this matters most to aren’t the ones learning JavaScript. They’re the career switcher who needs a structured path to something niche and employable. The lifelong learner who’s curious about something nobody has made a course about. The professional who wants to go deep on one specific skill and doesn’t have time for a course that covers everything else around it.

## What’s Actually Under the Hood

The short version: Next.js 16, React 19, Gemini for LLM inference, Prisma on a Postgres database, Tailwind for styling, Framer Motion for animations. JWT auth baked in from day one.

The slightly more interesting version: the entire design system is hand-built — no component library, no chart library. The visual language (hard offset shadows, warm neutrals, a single orange accent, buttons that physically press down on click) was built from scratch to feel tactile and a little playful, the same way Duolingo’s UI feels. That kind of design intentionality compounds. It’s the difference between an app that feels like a product and one that feels like a side project.

## The Bet

The core loop is live. The real question now is whether the engagement mechanics translate — whether someone learning negotiation or financial modeling gets the same “I can’t break my streak” pull that a Duolingo user does.

The hypothesis is yes. Because again, the streak isn’t about the content. It’s about identity. And identity is portable across subjects.

If that holds, the opportunity is genuinely large. Not just as a product, but as a different model for how people learn — one where the path is built for you specifically, the format keeps you engaged, and the content can be literally anything.

The graveyard of half-watched courses is a solvable problem. Beacon is a bet that this is how you solve it.

*Beacon is live and free to try. Built with Next.js 16, React 19, Gemini, and Prisma + Neon Postgres. Try it out *[*here*](https://beaconlearn.vercel.app/)*!*

02.title: SumTube: Turning YouTube Videos into Instant Summaries
02.author: Dierta Pasific
02.markdown:
### Turning Long Videos Into Bite-Sized Insights

We live in an era where YouTube has become the largest library of knowledge on the internet. From hour-long podcasts to educational lectures, it’s the go-to place for learning. But let’s be honest most of us don’t always have the time to sit through a 2-hour video just to capture the main points.

> SumTube transforms hours of spoken content into **digestible insight**

That’s exactly why SumTube was born: an AI-powered tool that fetches a YouTube transcript, breaks it down, and generates a clear, concise summary so you can save time and focus on what matters most.

Check it out here (En & Id): [Demo](https://sumtube.streamlit.app/)

### Why Build SumTube?

YouTube is the world’s largest video library, but ironically, also one of the hardest platforms to consume efficiently. Educational videos can stretch for hours, podcasts often bury valuable insights between casual conversations, and news explainers tend to include filler before reaching the core message.

For learners, researchers, and professionals, this easily turns into information overload. That’s why I built SumTube — a tool designed to save time by distilling long videos into concise summaries, provide clarity through bullet-point breakdowns, and even generate structured reports in PDF format for later use.

That’s where AI comes in.

### How SumTube Works

### Step 1 : User Input

The app extracts the video ID and pulls the transcript using the YouTube Transcript API.

### Step 2 : Transcript Fetching

Using the youtube-transcript-api, every spoken line is pulled and stitched into readable text.

### Step 3 : AI Summarization

The transcript is chunked into smaller segments. Each chunk is summarized using Hugging Face’s facebook/bart-large-cnn model. A second “multi-pass” summarization refines all chunk summaries into a final polished overview. Currently SumTube supports English and Indonesian videos.

### Step 4 : PDF Export

The results aren’t just on-screen. You can download a professional-looking PDF by using reportlab that contains the video title as the document title, sfinal summary and bullet point breakdowns.

### Step 5 : User Interface

Built with Streamlit, users can interact with two tabs: summary tab which contains final summary + bullet points + PDF download. And aranscript tab containing Full raw transcript for reference.

### Tech Stack

- Streamlit → for the web app interface.
- YouTube Transcript API → to fetch transcripts.
- Transformers (Hugging Face) → for summarization (BART model).
- PyTorch → as the backend for model inference.
- yt_dlp → for fetching YouTube metadata (like video title).
- ReportLab → for generating PDF reports.

### Final Thoughts

SumTube is my experiment in blending AI + video learning. Instead of watching a two-hour video, you can grab the essence in a neatly packaged summary and still dive into the transcript if needed.

It’s not meant to replace content, but to make learning more efficient.

The code is open-source, so feel free to clone, improve, or use it for your own workflow.

03.title: Cardify: LLM-Powered Flashcard Generator
03.author: Dierta Pasific
03.markdown:
### Instantly Turn Any PDF into AI-Generated Flashcards

Have you ever felt overwhelmed by the sheer volume of PDFs you need to study? Whether it’s a research paper, a textbook chapter, or a dense report, extracting key information and turning it into a memorable format is a tedious task. Manually creating flashcards is time-consuming and often distracts from the actual goal: learning.

To solve this problem, I built Cardify: a simple yet powerful web application that uses AI to automatically generate flashcards from any PDF document.

## What is Cardify?

Cardify is an app built with Streamlit and powered by the LLaMA 3 70B-Instruct language model, accessed through the lightning-fast Groq API. Just upload a PDF file, and with a single click, Cardify extracts the most important points and turns them into printable, easy-to-review flashcards.

The goal is simple: to automate the study process and make learning more efficient. Instead of spending hours reading and taking notes, you can get the core concepts of any material in a ready-to-use format.

You can try it out yourself [**here**](https://cardifyai.streamlit.app/)!

## How It Works: The Architecture Behind Cardify

The process behind Cardify is designed to be both effective and efficient, from text extraction to the final flashcard generation. Let’s break down the workflow.

### The User Interface: Built with Streamlit

The entire frontend is a simple Streamlit interface. Streamlit allows for rapid development of data-centric web apps purely in Python. The UI consists of:

1. An st.file_uploader to accept PDF files.
2. An st.button to trigger the generation process.
3. A display area where the generated flashcards are shown, styled with a bit of custom HTML.
4. An st.download_button to save the flashcards as a clean PDF.

To ensure a smooth user experience, Cardify uses st.session_state to cache data like the extracted text and the generated cards, preventing re-runs and loss of data on UI interaction.

### Text Extraction & Chunking (utils.py)

First, the uploaded PDF needs to be read. I used the PyPDF library for this. To handle large documents without overwhelming the language model's context window, the text is extracted in "chunks."

The extract_text_per_chunk function reads the PDF page by page and groups the text into chunks of a specified number of pages (e.g., 10 pages per chunk). This ensures that even very large PDFs can be processed reliably.

```
# From utils.py
from pypdf import PdfReader

def extract_text_per_chunk(pdf_path, pages_per_chunk=10):
    reader = PdfReader(pdf_path)
    all_chunks = []
    # Loop through pages and group them into chunks
    for i in range(0, len(reader.pages), pages_per_chunk):
        chunk = ""
        for j in range(i, min(i + pages_per_chunk, len(reader.pages))):
            chunk += reader.pages[j].extract_text() or ""
        all_chunks.append(chunk.strip())
    return all_chunkspy
```

### The AI Magic: A Two-Step Prompting Strategy (app.py & model.py)

This is where the core logic resides. Instead of asking the AI to create flashcards from raw, lengthy text, I implemented a two-step prompting strategy for better and more focused results.

> * Cardify uses Meta’s LLaMA 3 70B Instruct model, served via Groq’s ultra-low latency API, enabling rapid flashcard generation — even for large or complex PDFs.*

Step 1: Summarize Key Points The first prompt iterates through each text chunk and asks the model to identify and summarize the most important points. This turns a wall of text into a structured, bulleted list of key insights.

```
Dari teks berikut, identifikasi dan ringkas poin-poin penting yang
memuat informasi utama, insight bermakna, atau fakta signifikan.

• Sajikan dalam bentuk bullet point.
• Gunakan bahasa Indonesia yang formal, jelas, dan mudah dipahami.
• Setiap poin harus ringkas, padat, dan tidak mengulang informasi yang sama.
• Jangan menambahkan informasi yang tidak terdapat dalam teks.

Teks sumber:
"""
{text_chunk}
"""
```

Step 2: Generate Flashcards from Summaries After collecting the key points from all chunks, they are combined. A second, more specific prompt is then sent to the model, instructing it to turn these summarized points into flashcards. This prompt has very strict rules: one sentence per card, no Q&A format, and no introductory phrases. This ensures the output is clean and ready for use.

```
Dari teks berikut, buatlah daftar flashcard. Setiap flashcard harus berisi satu poin atau konsep kunci, diringkas dalam satu kalimat singkat dan padat.

{combined_notes}

Pisahkan setiap flashcard dengan dua baris kosong.
Jangan gunakan format tanya jawab.
Jangan sertakan awalan atau pembuka.
Pastikan setiap flashcard hanya berisi satu kalimat.
Gunakan Bahasa Indonesia.
```

### Final Output: Generating the PDF (app.py & ReportLab)

Once the flashcards are generated as a list of strings, the user needs a way to save them. I used the ReportLab library to dynamically create a PDF document from the flashcards. The code carefully formats each card, adds a title like "Card 1," and handles text wrapping to ensure the layout is clean and readable. The final PDF is served to the user via Streamlit's st.download_button.

## Conclusion and Future Ideas

Cardify is a testament to how modern AI tools can be harnessed to create practical applications that solve real-world problems. By combining the power of LLMs with the simplicity of Python libraries, we can build tools that genuinely improve our productivity and learning processes.

For the future, I’m considering a few enhancements:

- Support for other file types (e.g., .docx, .txt).
- Different flashcard formats, such as Question/Answer.
- Integration with spaced repetition systems like Anki.

04.title: Rupcara: Empowering the Visually Impaired with AI Money Recognition
04.author: Dierta Pasific
04.markdown:
## Rupcara: AI That Reads Money

### Empowering the Visually Impaired Through AI-Powered Currency Recognition

Imagine a world where visually impaired individuals can instantly recognize the value of their money just by showing it to a camera. This is the mission behind Rupcara — a deep learning project I developed to empower the visually impaired in recognizing Indonesian Rupiah banknotes using AI.

> *Rupcara is derived from the Indonesian phrase “Rupiah Bicara,” meaning “Rupiah Speaks.”*

The idea is simple yet powerful: to give a voice to money, making it accessible to everyone — especially those who rely more on touch and sound than on sight.

I’ve also created an interactive prototype of Rupcara using Streamlit, although it’s still in its early stages, you can try it out and see how Rupcara recognizes Indonesian Rupiah banknotes and converts them into spoken words.

Check it out here: [Demo](https://rupcara.streamlit.app/)

## Why Money Recognition Matters

For many visually impaired individuals, something as simple as recognizing the value of money can become a daily challenge. Most currencies, including the Indonesian Rupiah, lack tactile features that are easy to distinguish by touch, leaving many people to rely on memory, trust, or assistance from others.

This can lead to situations where visually impaired users may feel vulnerable, frustrated, or dependent when handling cash — whether paying at a store, receiving change, or managing their finances.

While some existing solutions, such as specialized banknote readers, do exist, they are often costly, bulky, or not easily accessible to everyone. This gap inspired me to explore how AI and computer vision could create a more inclusive, practical, and affordable solution.

## Rupcara User Flow: Explained

### Step 1: User Input

The user holds a Rupiah banknote in front of the camera. This is the starting point, where the user interacts directly with the system. No buttons or complex actions are needed — just show the money.

### Step 2: Image Capture

The camera captures an image of the banknote. This step is crucial because the quality of the image (lighting, angle, clarity) affects the accuracy of recognition.

### Step 3: Image Processing

Before the AI model can recognize the banknote, the system processes the captured image. This includes:

- Resizing the image to a fixed size (224x224 pixels).
- Normalizing pixel values for better model performance.
- Converting the image into a tensor format that the AI model can understand.

This preprocessing ensures consistent input for the model, regardless of the original image.

### Step 4: Recognition

The AI model analyzes features from the image — like patterns, colors, and textures — and predicts the denomination of the banknote. This is where AI-powered learning comes into play, using patterns it has learned from training data.

### Step 5: Voice Output

Once the model predicts the denomination, the result is converted into spoken words using a text-to-speech (TTS) engine. For example, if the model predicts “10.000 Rupiah,” the system prepares the spoken output:
  “Nominal sepuluh ribu Rupiah”

### Step 6: Feedback to User

The app speaks the denomination aloud, giving the user instant feedback. This audio confirmation allows the user to know the value of the banknote without needing visual cues, empowering them to handle money independently.

## What’s Behind Rupcara

At its core, Rupcara is a fusion of artificial intelligence, computer vision, and audio feedback — designed to bridge the gap between money and accessibility. By turning visual information into spoken words, Rupcara empowers visually impaired users to recognize banknotes independently.

Building Rupcara required careful integration of several technologies, from deep learning for recognition, to computer vision for image processing, to text-to-speech (TTS) for audio feedback. Here’s an overview of the key components that make Rupcara work.

### Deep Learning Model: ResNet-18

The heart of the system lies in ResNet-18, a deep learning model well-known for its balance between accuracy and efficiency. I fine-tuned this model, which was originally trained on ImageNet, to classify 23 different classes of Indonesian Rupiah banknotes. The training data combined several datasets from Kaggle, featuring banknotes from multiple years including 2011, 2016, and 2022, to ensure broad coverage and robustness.

The training process involved resizing images to 224x224 pixels, normalizing pixel values, and replacing the final classification layer to match the Rupiah denominations. I trained the model over 20 epochs using the Adam optimizer and a batch size of 32, achieving high accuracy in classifying denominations under various lighting conditions and angles.

### Text-to-Speech (TTS): gTTS

After making a prediction, Rupcara generates spoken feedback using gTTS (Google Text-to-Speech). This allows the app to say the denomination out loud in Bahasa Indonesia, enhancing the user experience and making it accessible for users who might have visual impairments.

### Web Application Framework: Streamlit

The entire application runs on Streamlit, a Python framework that allows for rapid development of interactive web apps. Streamlit makes it easy to integrate image uploads, model predictions, and audio playback into a clean, intuitive interface — no web development required!

### Supporting Libraries

- Torchvision for image preprocessing and model utilities
- PIL (Python Imaging Library) for image handling
- Matplotlib and Seaborn used in earlier analysis and visualization phases
- PyTorch for deep learning model building and training

## Handling Negative Cases

No model is perfect, and real-world users can upload anything — from random objects to handwritten notes. That’s why a critical part of Rupcara’s design is handling negative cases: images that aren’t actually Indonesian Rupiah.

When a user uploads a picture of, say, a flower or a cup of coffee, Rupcara needs to detect that it’s *not* a valid banknote. Instead of giving a false prediction (like mistaking a floral pattern for a security feature on a banknote), the model returns a special class: Unknown.

This behavior is made possible by including an Unknown class in the training dataset. During model training, we deliberately introduced a variety of images that are *not* Rupiah, teaching the model to distinguish between what *is* a banknote and what isn’t. This approach helps reduce false positives and improves the app’s reliability in practical use.

Here’s how the app responds when it encounters an image it doesn’t recognize:

- It shows a warning message explaining that the uploaded image could not be identified as a valid Indonesian Rupiah.
- It plays an audio response using text-to-speech (TTS), letting the user know to try a clearer or valid image of the currency.

This negative case handling makes Rupcara more robust, user-friendly, and realistic for real-world scenarios. After all, not every user will always upload perfect pictures of banknotes!

## Final Thoughts

Through Rupcara, I hope to show how the power of AI, combined with a passion for solving real-world problems, can lead to meaningful impact. Behind the name “Rupcara” — lies a vision: to make currency recognition more accessible and user-friendly for everyone, especially those who may benefit from voice-assisted technology.

This project is just the beginning. I believe with continued learning and collaboration, we can build tools that truly make a difference. Whether you’re a fellow developer, an AI enthusiast, or someone exploring the intersection of technology and inclusivity — I hope Rupcara inspires you to keep creating, learning, and contributing.

chatdp.title: ChatDP: AI-Powered Portfolio Chatbot
chatdp.author: Dierta Pasific
chatdp.markdown:
### Bringing My Portfolio to Life with an Interactive AI Chatbot

A portfolio website is designed to showcase who you are, what you do, and what you’re capable of — but I wanted mine to go beyond just displaying my work. I wanted it to reflect my skills in a way that was both innovative and interactive.

> I wanted my portfolio to be an experience, not just a showcase.

That’s when I decided to build an AI-powered portfolio website. Instead of a static page, visitors could now ask questions about me, making the experience more dynamic and engaging. But beyond just being a cool feature, this project became a hands-on way for me to explore AI, particularly NLP and experiment with real-world applications.

## How ChatDP Works

### Step 1: User Input — Start the Conversation

The interaction begins when a user types a question into the chatbot interface. Unlike traditional portfolio websites that rely on static content, ChatDP allows visitors to engage dynamically by asking direct questions about my work, experience, or projects. This makes the experience more interactive and personalized.

### Step 2: Text Processing — Understanding Your Question

Once you hit enter, the chatbot gets to work. Using **Sentence Transformers**, it converts your question into a numerical format called an **embedding**, which captures the meaning behind the words. This allows ChatDP to analyze your question beyond just keywords.

### Step 3: Similarity Matching — Finding the Best Answer

ChatDP doesn’t just pull up random answers. It compares your question’s embedding against a pre-processed JSON dataset of questions and answers. Using **cosine similarity**, it measures how closely your query matches past questions, ensuring you get the most relevant response.

### Step 4: Best Match Selection — Picking the Right Response

With the similarity scores calculated, ChatDP selects the most relevant answer. If it finds a strong match, the chatbot is ready to deliver an accurate response. But if the match is weak, it won’t guess blindly — it’s designed to avoid misinformation.

### Step 5: Response Display — A Seamless Conversation

Finally, the chatbot presents the best answer in a conversational format. Instead of navigating through endless pages, visitors get direct, AI-powered insights — making my portfolio more engaging, informative, and interactive.

You can try it out yourself [**here**](https://diertapasific.github.io/)!

## The Technologies Behind the Chatbot

Choosing the right set of tools for my chatbot was essential. I wanted something lightweight that could run directly in the browser while still processing text efficiently.

After evaluating different options, I decided on Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime for ChatDP. This combination allowed me to handle text processing on the client-side, eliminating the need for external servers and ensuring a fast, scalable solution.

### Transformers: The Core of NLP

For ChatDP, I used **Sentence Transformers** from Hugging Face, a library designed for tasks like semantic textual similarity. Instead of generating new responses, my chatbot retrieves the most relevant answer from a predefined dataset.

To achieve this, I fine-tuned the **all-MiniLM-L6-v2** model on my dataset of questions and answers. The goal was to make the model **better at matching similar questions** by adjusting how it represents text as numerical vectors (embeddings).

During fine-tuning, I used the **CosineSimilarityLoss** function, which teaches the model to bring similar questions and answers **closer together** in vector space. This way, when a user asks a question, ChatDP can find the most relevant response by comparing embeddings rather than relying on keyword matching.

Here’s a simplified look at the fine-tuning process

```
# Load Pretrained Sentence Transformer Model
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

# Convert Data into Training Examples
train_examples = [InputExample(texts=[item["question"], item["answer"]], label=1.0) for item in dataset]
train_dataloader = DataLoader(train_examples, shuffle=True, batch_size=4)

# Define Loss Function
train_loss = losses.CosineSimilarityLoss(model)

# Fine-Tune the Model
model.fit(train_objectives=[(train_dataloader, train_loss)], epochs=5, warmup_steps=100)
```

After fine-tuning, the chatbot follows these steps when answering a question:

- Convert user input into an embedding (vector representation).
- Compare the user’s embedding with precomputed question embeddings using cosine similarity to measure how closely they match.
- Retrieve the answer corresponding to the most similar question in the dataset.

This approach makes ChatDP lightweight and efficient, as it doesn’t generate text dynamically but instead provides accurate, pre-existing answers based on semantic similarity.

### ONNX Runtime: Running Efficient Models in the Browser

To make ChatDP run **directly in the browser** without relying on a backend server, I converted the fine-tuned model to **ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) format**. This allows the chatbot to process queries locally on a user’s device, improving speed and scalability.

ONNX Runtime optimizes and accelerates deep learning models for various platforms, including browsers and mobile devices. By using ONNX, I was able to:

- Reduce model size for faster loading.
- Optimize inference speed so responses are near-instantaneous.
- Run the chatbot efficiently on low-power devices without needing a GPU.

To deploy the chatbot efficiently, I first wrapped my fine-tuned model in a class that formats the inputs correctly before converting it to ONNX:

```
class ONNXWrapper(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, model):
        super(ONNXWrapper, self).__init__()
        self.model = model

    def forward(self, input_ids, attention_mask):
        inputs = {"input_ids": input_ids, "attention_mask": attention_mask}
        embeddings = self.model.forward(inputs)  # Convert input to vector representation
        return embeddings
```

Then, I used **torch.onnx.export()** to convert it to ONNX format:

```
torch.onnx.export(
    onnx_model,
    (dummy_input_ids, dummy_attention_mask),  
    "chatbot_model.onnx",  # Save as ONNX file
    export_params=True,
    opset_version=14
)
```

By converting the model to ONNX, I ensured that ChatDP could **run entirely in the browser** without an internet connection. This means users get **instant responses** without delays, and the chatbot remains **privacy-friendly**, as no data is sent to external servers.

## What’s Next for ChatDP?

The development of ChatDP doesn’t stop here. I have a structured plan to continuously improve its performance and capabilities:

- **Build a Monitoring Pipeline & Dashboard** — Create a system to track key metrics like unanswered queries percentage and response quality.
- **Analyze Current Performance** — Use monitoring data to understand weaknesses in the current setup and identify areas for improvement.
- **Expand the Dataset** — Add more relevant data to improve the chatbot’s accuracy and coverage.
- **Switch to a Smaller LLM** — Transition to a lightweight language model that can run efficiently on a personal laptop CPU.
- **Iterate with Prompt Engineering** — Refine responses through improved prompts instead of just expanding the dataset.

## Wrapping Up: The Journey of Building ChatDP

Building ChatDP has been an exciting journey — one that blends AI, NLP, and web development into an interactive portfolio experience. What started as a simple idea to make my website more engaging turned into a hands-on exploration of fine-tuning transformer models, optimizing for browser-based inference, and deploying an AI assistant that truly reflects my work.

But this is just the beginning. With plans to improve accuracy, expand the dataset, and experiment with smaller LLMs, ChatDP will continue to evolve. If you’re as excited about AI and NLP as I am, I’d love to hear your thoughts — let’s connect and discuss how we can push the boundaries of interactive AI together!

Try [**ChatDP**](https://diertapasific.github.io/)** **now and see AI in action!

mobile-development.title: Introduction to Mobile App Development
mobile-development.author: Dierta Pasific
mobile-development.markdown:
## Getting Started with Mobile App Development: A Beginner’s Guide

### Dive into Mobile App Development

## Introduction

Mobile app development is the process of creating software applications that are designed to run on mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets. These applications, commonly known as mobile apps, serve various purposes, from enhancing productivity and communication to entertainment even gaming. Mobile app development can be a complex but rewarding, as it allows developers to reach a broad and diverse user base across different platforms.

## Mobile App Development Platforms

Mobile app development platforms are software tools that enable developers to create mobile applications for various operating systems like iOS, Android, and Windows. There are two primary categories of mobile app development:

### Native App Development Platforms

Native platforms are specifically designed and optimized for a particular mobile operating system, such as iOS or Android. When using native platforms, several advantages come into play. Native apps typically offer superior performance, characterized by faster responsiveness, and direct access to the device’s hardware and features.

### Cross-Platform App Development Platforms

Cross-platform platforms, on the other hand, facilitate the development of a single codebase that can be utilized across multiple mobile operating systems. Developers can create applications more efficiently because they only need to maintain one codebase, which can be deployed on multiple mobile platforms.

## Mobile App Development Tools

In mobile app development, the essential software tools and utilities encompass Android Studio and Xcode for native Android and iOS app development using Java, Kotlin, Objective-C, or Swift. Additionally, for cross-platform development, React Native (a JavaScript framework) and Flutter (a language introduced by Google in May 2017) are prominent choices, offering efficiency and flexibility in the design, coding, testing, and publishing of mobile applications.

## Challenges in Mobile App Development

Developing mobile applications entails several challenges that can impede progress. Firstly, achieving compatibility across various platforms is a constant struggle for developers. Ensuring the security of the application is another prominent challenge, given the need to protect user data in a hostile digital landscape. Additionally, optimizing application performance and resource management remains an ongoing concern. After completing the development process, there is the challenge of publishing the application and competing with other players in the app marketplace. These challenges highlight the complex nature of mobile app development, necessitating technical expertise and strategic thinking for successful navigation.

## Resources for Learning Mobile App Development

The vast expanse of the internet has made it increasingly accessible to acquire skills in mobile app development. Online learning platforms like Udemy and Coursera, as well as YouTube, offer a plethora of lessons tailored to both novice and proficient learners. Additionally, robust developer communities such as Stack Overflow and Reddit provide invaluable peer support to address challenges encountered during the app development journey.

> You don’t learn to walk by following rules. You learn by doing, and by falling over.

For beginners, an immensely effective strategy involves learning through practical engagement and active mobile application development. This method extends beyond mere theoretical comprehension, allowing individuals to gain hands-on experience in crafting real-world applications.
